A simple daily checklist to help you remember the basics. It starts fresh each day; use Progress for dated notes. These are educational steps, not a prescribed treatment plan.
Use a gentle cleanser when needed; avoid scrubbing.
Choose a moisturizer that feels comfortable and does not irritate.
Use shade and clothing; consider broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen when outdoors.
Remove daily dirt and sunscreen without harsh scrubbing.
Keep the routine simple; introduce only one new product at a time.
If symptoms persist or worsen, or you have a severe reaction, seek professional advice. Do not use household bleach or unreviewed whitening mixtures.

A small educational catalogue. Learn about common skincare ingredients and their limitations; this is not a product endorsement.
A humectant used in many moisturizers to help attract and hold water in the outer skin layer.
Caution: product formulation matters; choose a suitable finished product rather than applying concentrated raw ingredients.
Skin-identical lipids used in moisturizers to support the skin barrier and reduce moisture loss.
Caution: products vary; fragrance or other ingredients may still irritate some people.
A form of vitamin B3 used in some cosmetic products for barrier support and appearance-related benefits.
Caution: higher concentrations are not automatically better; stop use if irritation occurs.
Added to scent a product and may be listed under several names depending on the label.
Caution: fragrance can trigger irritation or allergy in some people; fragrance-free may be preferable for sensitive skin.
Kitchen lemon juice is not a tested skincare treatment and can irritate skin.
Avoid applying lemon juice to skin, especially before sunlight. It is not a safe DIY whitening method.
A finished sunscreen labelled broad-spectrum helps protect against UVA and UVB when used as directed.
Caution: use enough and reapply as directed on the label; shade and clothing also help. Availability and prices are not verified here.
Use only in a tested, labelled sunscreen
A humectant used in finished skincare products to help bind water in the outer skin layer.
Caution: results depend on the whole formulation; it does not replace a moisturizer or treat every cause of dryness. Stop if irritation occurs.
An occlusive ingredient used in ointments and moisturizers to reduce water loss from the skin.
Caution: use a finished product intended for skin. Texture and suitability vary; stop if the product causes irritation.
A form of vitamin B5 used in some finished products as a skin-conditioning and moisture-supporting ingredient.
Caution: formulations differ and ingredient presence does not guarantee a product will suit you. Stop if irritation occurs.
Finely milled oat material used in some finished skin-protectant and moisturizing products.
Caution: avoid products containing oats if you have a known oat allergy; stop if a reaction occurs.
A mineral UV-filter ingredient used in some finished sunscreens.
Caution: do not mix raw zinc oxide powder into homemade sunscreen. Use a tested, labelled broad-spectrum sunscreen and follow its directions.

A safer plan for uneven tone, tanning and dark marks
This section focuses on fading excess pigmentation and preventing new dark marks. It does not try to change your natural skin colour or promise a particular shade.
What would you like to improve?
Dark marks after acne can take months to fade. Preventing new breakouts and avoiding irritation are important; harsh scrubs and aggressive spot treatments can make marks worse.
Tanning is a response to UV exposure. Consistent sun protection is the foundation; a cosmetic product cannot reliably cancel ongoing unprotected sun exposure.

Persistent, spreading, symmetric or recurring patches may have causes such as melasma or another skin condition. A selfie or this questionnaire cannot identify the cause; arrange a clinician or dermatologist assessment before using strong lightening treatments.
Start with gentle skin care and sun protection. If darkening is new, changing, widespread or unexplained, get it assessed rather than guessing with multiple products.
Use a gentle cleanser if needed, then a moisturizer your skin tolerates. Avoid scrubbing or trying to peel the skin lighter.

Use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every morning on exposed skin. Reapply about every 2 hours outdoors and after swimming or heavy sweating. A tinted sunscreen containing iron oxides may help with visible-light-related pigmentation if you can find a shade that suits you. Hats and shade add protection.

Cleanse gently and moisturize. Keep the routine simple while your skin is irritated. Add no more than one new leave-on product at a time, follow its label, and stop if it burns, swells, or causes a rash.
Ingredients to research — not a prescription

Dermatology guidance lists options such as azelaic acid, vitamin C, glycolic acid, kojic acid and retinoids for selected dark spots. Suitability depends on the cause and your skin. Start only with a clearly labelled product from a reliable source; do not combine several strong actives or use prescription medicines without a clinician.
Do not use dangerous whitening shortcuts

Avoid mercury-containing or unlabelled fairness creams, liquid bleach, steroid-mixed fairness creams, unknown imported mixtures, lemon juice, baking soda and abrasive scrubs. Do not self-start hydroquinone or prescription retinoids. Mercury and inappropriate lightening products can cause serious or lasting harm.

Dark marks often take 6–12 months to fade and deeper pigmentation can take longer. Progress is gradual, and new marks can appear if the trigger continues. The goal is a more even return toward your natural tone, not a guaranteed lighter complexion.

This is general educational guidance, not a diagnosis or a personalized treatment prescription. Seek medical advice for painful, itchy, rapidly changing, spreading or persistent patches, or if a product causes a significant reaction.

High risk: water-based homemade mixtures can grow bacteria, yeast and mould. Without a validated preservative system, suitable pH, clean manufacturing and stability plus microbial testing, do not store or use them. Refrigeration and a short shelf life do not make them reliably safe.

Lower water-related microbial risk does not mean risk-free. Oils and butters can oxidize, trigger allergy or irritate skin; raw kitchen oils are not standardized cosmetic ingredients. Do not add water, fresh herbs or food. Prefer a properly labelled finished product.

Kitchen powders are not sterile or standardized. Scrubs can damage the skin barrier, and plant or food powders may irritate or trigger allergy. Do not use abrasive particles on the face or mix powders with water for storage.

Never make sunscreen at home. UV protection depends on validated filters, exact dispersion, formulation, testing and regulated labelling. Oils, zinc oxide powder or online recipes cannot provide a dependable SPF.

Do not apply an unknown mixture. Identify every ingredient and its cosmetic grade, concentration, compatibility, contamination risk and intended use first. If any of these are unknown, do not make it.

No homemade whitening recipe is recommended here. Avoid lemon, baking soda, bleach, toothpaste, harsh scrubs, mercury products and steroid-mixed fairness creams. A patch test cannot prove a formula is safe.

An ingredient used in some finished skincare products. The American Academy of Dermatology lists azelaic acid among ingredients that may help fade existing dark spots; the cause of pigmentation still matters.
Caution: finished products can still sting or irritate. Do not apply raw cosmetic or laboratory material. Introduce only one new active at a time and stop if irritation occurs.
An alpha-hydroxy acid used in some finished exfoliating products. Dermatologists list it as one possible ingredient for fading dark spots, but suitability depends on the skin and formulation.

Caution: overuse or strong formulations can irritate skin and worsen post-inflammatory marks. Avoid DIY acid peels and raw ingredients; use sun protection and stop if burning or persistent irritation occurs.
A cosmetic ingredient used in some products marketed for uneven tone. The American Academy of Dermatology lists it among ingredients that may help fade dark spots.
Caution: it can cause irritation or contact allergy in some people. Use only a properly labelled finished cosmetic product; do not mix powders or improvise a home formula.

A family of vitamin-A-related ingredients used in skincare. Some retinoids are listed by dermatologists as options that may help fade dark spots, but different members have different strengths and legal/medical status.

Caution: dryness, peeling and irritation are possible and can worsen dark marks. Do not self-start prescription retinoids; avoid topical retinoids during pregnancy and ask a clinician if pregnant or planning pregnancy.
An antioxidant ingredient used in finished skincare products. The American Academy of Dermatology lists vitamin C among ingredients that may help fade existing dark spots.
Caution: vitamin C products differ in form, stability and acidity; some irritate skin. Do not make or store homemade vitamin C mixtures, and stop if irritation occurs.

These are possible ingredients in finished products, not a prescription or a promise of results. First address irritation or the underlying cause and use sun protection. All entries still require qualified review.
What responsible cosmetic formulation actually requires
A safe cosmetic is a tested system, not just a list of natural ingredients. These are the checks a qualified formulator must document before a product is used on skin.

Confirm the exact INCI or chemical identity, cosmetic-use grade, supplier traceability, batch number, specification and certificate of analysis. Food-grade, kitchen or unknown powders are not automatically suitable for cosmetics.

A percentage is meaningful only for a specific ingredient, grade, product type and complete formula. Check supplier limits, applicable cosmetic rules, interactions and total exposure. Do not estimate amounts from online recipes or combine multiple strong actives.

For water-containing products, pH can affect preservative performance, ingredient stability and skin tolerability. It must be measured with calibrated equipment using a validated method; guessing by colour or household strips is not a release test.

Water-based products require a preservative system proven effective in the exact formula and package. A preservative name or typical supplier use range alone does not prove protection. Hygiene, water quality and manufacturing controls also matter.

A qualified lab must assess physical and chemical stability, package compatibility and appropriate microbial quality/preservative-efficacy testing over the intended shelf life. Smell, appearance, refrigeration or a patch test cannot establish product safety.

Without ingredient documentation, a complete formula, validated preservation where needed, suitable testing and a qualified review, do not make or apply a homemade cosmetic. This app intentionally provides no mixing instructions, percentages, shelf-life claims or sunscreen recipes.

For more comparable progress photos: use the same camera and distance, face the camera straight on, use soft even light, avoid flash, direct sunlight and filters, and keep the time of day similar. These steps improve consistency but cannot turn photos into a skin analysis.
A private formulation worksheet for learning the arithmetic of a small batch. It does not recommend a recipe or verify ingredient safety.
Only the water-free worksheet is enabled. Water-free does not automatically mean safe: use only documented cosmetic-grade materials and obtain qualified formulation review before applying.

Water-based serums and creams are disabled for home formulation here. They need a validated preservative system, measured pH, controlled manufacturing, stability and microbial testing for the exact formula and package.
DIY sunscreen formulation is disabled. Never rely on homemade sunscreen, oils or loose UV-filter powders for sun protection.
